passage: I'm Farida, and looking back at the class picnic last month, I can see how I was. I made the plan, the list, the timings, even who sat next to whom on the bus. When Irfan suggested we stop at the lake first, I cut him off: "No, that'll ruin the schedule." I didn't even listen. I rewrote everyone's food list because they'd "do it wrong". By lunchtime, nobody was talking to me much. Irfan said, "It's like we're all just in your plan." That stung. The truth is, when I'm not in charge, my stomach knots up. I keep imagining the bus breaking down or someone getting lost. Next trip, I'm going to let Irfan plan one part. Even if it goes a bit wrong.

qa.q: Where did Irfan suggest stopping first?
qa.a: He suggested stopping at the lake first.

qa.q: What is Farida afraid of when not in charge?
qa.a: Farida's stomach knots up with fear of things going wrong, like the bus breaking down or someone getting lost.

qa.q: What choice is Farida planning for the next trip, and why might it help?
qa.a: Farida plans to let Irfan plan one part, practising letting go even if it goes a bit wrong, so others feel heard.

qa.q: How did Irfan experience the picnic?
qa.a: He felt unheard, saying it was like they were all just in Farida's plan.

grounding: A teenager looks back on controlling every picnic detail, sees the fear behind it and how it left classmates feeling unheard.

passage:
Project mentor's note, Mehak, Class 10 science exhibition.
Dhruv has taken over his group's solar-car model completely. He assigns every task, redoes wiring others have done and says "Just let me" a lot. When Anjali tried to paint the chassis, he took the brush from her. Today I asked him to step back for one hour while the group chose the colour scheme. He paced and kept glancing over, clearly anxious. Afterwards he admitted, "I'm scared it'll fail and it'll be my fault." That helped me understand him. His teammates have gone very quiet this week.
Next step: each member now owns one part, and Dhruv leads only the testing. We check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Dhruv take from Anjali?
qa.a: He took the brush from her when she tried to paint the chassis.

qa.q: What is Dhruv afraid of that makes him take over everything?
qa.a: He's scared the model will fail and it will be his fault.

qa.q: What choice did Mehak make to help the group, and why?
qa.a: Mehak gave each member one part to own and limited Dhruv to leading the testing, so others are heard and Dhruv practises letting go.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's teammates feel before Friday's check-in?
qa.a: They had gone quiet and probably felt unheard, but owning their own parts may help them feel included again.

grounding: A mentor notes a teenager who takes charge of everything out of fear of failure, leaving teammates unheard, and gives each member ownership.

passage:
Rehana,
I owe you a proper apology, so I'm writing it. At the class picnic I planned everything: the bus, the food, who sat where, which games. When you suggested going to the lake instead of the fort, I said no before you'd finished. Then I corrected how you packed the sandwiches. In front of everyone. You went quiet the rest of the day, and I only understood why when Pooja said you felt like a passenger at your own picnic. The truth is, when I'm not in charge, my stomach ties itself in knots, as if something will go wrong and it will be my fault. That's my stuff, not yours. Next time, will you plan half? I'll try not to fix it.
Bhavna

qa.q: Where did Rehana want to go instead of the fort?
qa.a: To the lake.

qa.q: What does Bhavna feel when not in charge?
qa.a: Bhavna feels anxious, stomach in knots, afraid something will go wrong and be Bhavna's fault.

qa.q: What small step does Bhavna offer to change the pattern?
qa.a: Letting Rehana plan half of the next outing and trying not to fix it.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel at the picnic?
qa.a: Rehana felt unheard, like a passenger at the picnic, and went quiet.

grounding: Shows a teen who takes over every plan and corrects others out of anxiety, leaving a friend feeling unheard.

passage: You want to know why I gave up the football captaincy? It wasn't the coach. It was me. I'm Omkar, Class 10, and I was the kind of captain who told everyone where to stand, how to kick, when to drink water. Rukmini, our goalkeeper, finally said in front of the whole team, "You never ask us anything." I was furious. Then I went home and couldn't sleep, because she was right. If I wasn't controlling every pass, I felt the whole match would fall apart and it would be my fault. That's fear, not leadership. So I gave the armband to her for a month. Hardest month of my life. We won two matches, lost one. I survived.

qa.q: Who said "You never ask us anything"?
qa.a: Rukmini, the goalkeeper.

qa.q: What was Omkar afraid of when not controlling every pass?
qa.a: Omkar feared the match would fall apart and it would be Omkar's fault.

qa.q: Which choice helped Omkar most, and why?
qa.a: Handing the armband to Rukmini for a month, which showed things could go on without total control.

qa.q: How might the team have felt under Omkar as captain?
qa.a: The team probably felt unheard and bossed around, since they were never asked for ideas.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who controls every play out of fear, leaves teammates unheard and tries letting someone else lead.

passage:
Monday: Aadhya made the group-study timetable for the four of them, colour-coded, and sent it before anyone asked. When Sangeeta suggested starting with history, Aadhya replied, "No, maths first, it's more logical," and felt her heart race until Sangeeta agreed.
Thursday: At study group, Aadhya corrected how Sangeeta wrote her notes, twice. Sangeeta packed up early. Later she texted, "Do you even want our ideas?" Aadhya stared at the message, stomach sick.
The next Sunday: Aadhya asked the group, "What should we start with?" and made herself sit through the pause. Sangeeta chose history. Aadhya's hands fidgeted under the table, but the session went fine.

qa.q: What subject did Sangeeta choose on Sunday?
qa.a: History.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel reading Sangeeta's text?
qa.a: She felt sick with worry and guilt, realising her control had hurt her friend.

qa.q: What did Aadhya try on Sunday, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: She asked the group and sat through the pause, letting others lead despite her nerves.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel on Thursday?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt unheard and corrected, so she packed up early and questioned whether her ideas were wanted.

grounding: Shows over several days a teen who controls plans out of anxiety, learns friends feel unheard and practises letting go.

passage:
Divyansh, you want everyone's trip to go your way, na? Your Bidisha Pishi was the same at sixteen. Let me tell you.
For our class picnic, I made the whole plan: the bus times, the menu, who sat where. When Tapas suggested the riverbank instead of the fort, I said, "No, I've already decided." When Mitali packed the sandwiches, I re-wrapped every one because she'd done it "wrong".
My stomach was in knots the whole week. What if the bus was late? What if it rained? If I wasn't in charge, it felt like everything would fall apart.
On the picnic day, Mitali sat with other girls and wouldn't talk to me. That night she said, "You never listen to anyone." That hurt, because she was right.
The next outing, I chose one thing to plan, the games. The rest, I let others decide. It was scary. And it was the best picnic we had.

qa.q: What did Tapas suggest instead of the fort?
qa.a: The riverbank.

qa.q: What was young Bidisha feeling during the week before the picnic?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with her stomach in knots, afraid everything would fall apart if she wasn't in charge.

qa.q: What choice did young Bidisha make for the next outing, and why did it help?
qa.a: She planned only the games and let others decide the rest, which made space for friends to be heard and led to the best picnic.

qa.q: How did Mitali feel about the re-wrapped sandwiches and the plans?
qa.a: Mitali felt unheard and hurt, saying, "You never listen to anyone," and sat with other girls on the picnic day.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling how, as a teen, fear of things going wrong made her control every plan until a friend felt unheard, and how she let go a little.
